meta.headline: NEW (2026-07-09) — THE WEDGE IS COMPLIANCE. Live advisor research (design-partner onboarding, 2026-07-08) confirmed the real buying gate: an advisor cannot put client data into ChatGPT, and compliance approval comes BEFORE any interest in features. Lantern's local-first architecture IS the answer to that #1 pain — so the pitch now leads with it: 'The AI you're actually allowed to use with client data.' Everything about the client stays on the advisor's own machine; answers come with citations. Current thrust: (1) a polished Compliance & Security pack an advisor can hand straight to their compliance officer (the gate-opener), (2) a reframed onboarding that leads with the compliance answer, (3) closing Jump feature-parity where it matters — calendar/scheduling + account-opening prefill — as a simple, AI-first app, NOT a 'connect 60 things' note-taker. Go-to-market is design-partner-led and XYPN-approved-list first. This refines the 2026-06-29 'compete head-on as the leading, simple, AI-first advisor app' stance (still in force); it does NOT retreat to a niche.

sections.title: Strategy & Vision
sections.now: Compliance is now the wedge: live advisor research on 2026-07-08 showed the first buying gate is 'can we use it?' before 'what does it do?' Lantern leads with 'The AI you're actually allowed to use with client data': local-first, cited answers, and client files kept on the advisor's own machine. Lantern is the internal name for the platform; advisors see the product as **Advisor Prep Hero** (advisorprephero.com). The 2026-06-29 stance still holds: compete head-on with Jump as a simple, powerful, AI-first advisor app, not a note-taker; start with solo and small fee-only RIAs; make local-first the proof, not a slogan.
decisions: BOARD DIRECTION (2026-06-29, still in force): compete head-on to be the leading financial-advisor AI, not a retreat to a niche. Position as a simple, powerful AI app: connect your files, ask cited questions, get a living Client Map. Notetaking is a feature at most, never the identity.
RE-AIM (2026-06-24): the lead market is financial advisors; the user-facing unit is client / household, while the internal isolation engine keeps matter / matter_id unchanged.
Research decision (2026-07-08): compliance is the first buying gate. The pitch must answer 'can we use it?' before asking the advisor to care about features.
Lead with the new line: 'The AI you're actually allowed to use with client data.' That names the ChatGPT problem and turns local-first architecture into the buying reason.
Build the Compliance & Security pack as the CCO gate-opener and wire it into onboarding with a 'For your compliance officer' call-to-action.
Go-to-market path: design partner first, then her firm, then peers, then XYPN approved-list, firm references, and compliance-consultant channels such as Synergy Compliance.
Demo-first still stands: show a reliable clean-slate advisor flow before asking for wider adoption. Build only what advances that path or the compliance gate.
insights: Firsthand Jump read remains the competitive opening: Jump is the visible incumbent, but Jameson found its AI scattered and still organized around notes and forms. Lantern should win by being simpler, clearer, and AI-first.
The 2026-07-08 advisor research exposed a two-step buying model: compliance first, product value second. The design partner would have stopped at the AI-key screen without a compliance answer.

Local-first is a structural advantage because client files can stay on the advisor's device instead of on a software vendor's server. It reduces the vendor-data problem, though cloud AI providers still need firm approval when client content is sent to them.
The advisor's lived enemy is 'putting client data into ChatGPT.' Consumer names matter in copy: say ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), and Gemini (Google), not only provider-company names.
The onboarding story should explain what the product is in one sentence, make the tour re-findable, and show the Compliance & Security pack before the advisor invests time in setup.
North Star remains weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow, not signups or feature count.

sections.title: Competitive & Market
sections.now: The market read is now sharper: Lantern competes head-on with Jump, but not by becoming a bigger note-taker or a “connect 60 things” hub. The opening is a simple AI-first product that an advisor can actually get approved to use with client data, backed by local-first architecture and citations.
decisions: Keep the 2026-06-29 head-on stance: be the leading simple advisor AI, not a niche retreat and not a note-taking clone.
Close Jump parity where it matters for the buyer: scheduling/calendar and account-opening prefill, while keeping the product simpler and more AI-first.
Use compliance-led differentiation against cloud notetakers: local client files, firm-controlled AI account/key, visible data flow, and CCO materials.
Keep connector breadth honest: live connection, export folder, and prepare-and-handoff are all valid modes; do not promise blocked partner integrations as if they are already live.
insights: Jameson’s firsthand Jump read remains useful: Jump has adoption, but its AI is scattered in the product and still tied to notes, forms, and workflows.
The advisor research validates the compliance difference: the default blocked tool in the advisor’s mind is ChatGPT with client data.
Jump’s XYPN path is a clue, not trivia. Trusted-list access can be more important than ordinary marketing for small RIAs.
Schwab and other custodian integrations have two layers: useful prepare/prefill work can happen now, while true one-click partner integrations require long approval paths.
FutureVault and other vault-style tools remain market intel, but the current product is an AI-first client intelligence app, not a document vault.

sections.title: Compliance & Security
sections.now: Compliance approval is the first buying gate. Lantern's local-first design is the structural answer: client files stay on the advisor's machine by default, the firm controls which AI provider and key are used, and the advisor gets a pack they can hand to their compliance officer. The SEC/RIA research says the concrete bar is the 2024 Reg S-P amendments; there is no explicit AI-software rule, but vendor review, safeguards, incident response, and recordkeeping still matter. The target reviewer pattern is a CCO or an outside consultant such as Synergy Compliance.
decisions: Build a polished CCO-facing Compliance & Security pack and keep it as the onboarding gate-opener; the draft lives under docs/partnerships/compliance-pack/ in the Lantern app repo.
Use the compliance pack and video script to answer 'can we use it?' before asking the advisor to evaluate product value.
Defer SOC 2 until a real deal demands it. Until then, lead with the truthful local-first story and a complete security questionnaire posture.
Avoid overclaims: do not say SEC-approved, compliant by default, no vendor review needed, or no data ever leaves unless every mode proves it.
insights: Provide a data-flow memo and diagram: local files, local index, AI prompts, provider routing, telemetry, support access, update checks, and subprocessors.
Provide a security controls packet: encryption at rest and in transit, key storage, permissions, update process, vulnerability handling, backup/deletion behavior, and support limits.
Provide an AI-use packet: supported providers, what data is sent, training posture, prompt construction, citations, hallucination controls, and human approval rules.

Provide vendor-due-diligence material: SOC 2 status or substitute evidence, security questionnaire, incident-response policy, business continuity summary, insurance, subprocessors, retention, and a security contact.
Provide incident and notice language: severity levels, investigation process, customer-information impact review, vendor notice timing, and the facts a firm needs for customer notice.
Provide records and retention guidance: where AI chats, drafts, citations, approvals, exports, and audit logs live; how advisors archive, search, and delete them.
Provide CCO-ready policy language and an XYPN/trusted-list packet, because curated-tech approval is partly a compliance-confidence sale.

sections.title: Engineering
sections.now: The app is functionally solid on Windows after bench testing; current engineering is closing the Jump gaps that matter and hardening the release path. The active build thrust is calendar write/scopes/booking domain, Schwab account-opening prefill through 8 account-type field maps, and the final signed installer path after Tauri version alignment.
decisions: Reuse the existing engine and keep matter / matter_id untouched internally; use client / household only as the user-facing label.

Calendar booking should use Option A: a privacy-preserving public booking page that stores only safe availability data such as advisor slug, bookable windows, and busy/free snapshots, never client files or notes.
Calendar parity needs new write permissions, user reconnect, event creation/update commands, meeting-link creation, and a booking model; existing calendar support is read-only.
Schwab parity starts with useful prefilled paperwork and handoff, while the one-click Schwab Digital Account Opening path remains a long partner-approval track.
Connector strategy shifts from “blocked” to three honest modes: live connection, export folder, and prepare-and-handoff.
insights: Existing pieces help the booking work: Outlook/Google/iCloud calendar read, email send, UTC time handling, and the firm backend all exist; availability rules and public booking are the missing pieces.
Schwab data has near-term paths through aggregators such as Plaid, Yodlee, and ByAllAccounts, but production access and consent handling still need clean review.
Official Schwab PDFs and prepare-and-handoff flows are feasible now; submitting directly through Schwab requires Schwab-approved paths.
Many gated connectors have a practical first version through customer credentials, file exports, or report folders; advisor data should be met where it already lives.
Release hardening is still real work: Azure Trusted Signing has been validated, but the final signed cut waits on the version-align fix.

sections.title: Design & UX
sections.now: Two rounds of feedback overhaul shipped, and the app is simpler, clearer, and back on the Advisor Prep Hero brand. The design system docs were refreshed after the overhaul. The onboarding reframe is not a new visual direction; it keeps the liked screens and changes the story so compliance comes before setup.
decisions: Keep the polished light theme. No dark-mode work unless Jameson explicitly asks for it.
Keep the shared design primitives and unified tokens so surfaces look like one product, including the unified rail width.
Use the swappable brand system: Lantern is the internal platform name; Advisor Prep Hero is the advisor-facing product brand.
Onboarding keeps the restored visuals but adds the compliance beat, the CCO CTA, consumer provider names, a shield/on-device icon, and a re-findable tour.
Keep trust visible in the interface with data-flow language, citations, and the egress indicator.
insights: The visual overhaul fixed the broad product feel; the next design risk is story order, not styling.
The advisor research showed that vague benefit language confused the buyer. The first screen must say what the product is and what problem it solves.
Cloud AI copy needs care: both BYOK cloud and local modes should feel safe; local is the maximum-privacy option, not the only non-scary option.
Connector logos and familiar product names help advisors categorize the tool quickly.
A fiduciary reads sloppy UI as vendor risk, so polish is part of the trust story.

sections.title: Marketing
sections.now: Marketing now leads with the compliance answer, not generic AI value. The public promise is Advisor Prep Hero as 'The AI you're actually allowed to use with client data,' backed by local-first architecture, cited answers, and the CCO pack. The scalable channel target is the XYPN approved list, with design-partner proof, herd-adoption logos, Microsoft-adjacent trust, and compliance-consultant confidence.
decisions: Make the compliance wedge the front door: local-first, advisor-controlled AI account/key, cited answers, and a pack for the CCO.
Use the design partner path first, then her firm, then peers; do not pretend there is broad market proof before those users exist.
Pursue the XYPN approved-list path as the scalable channel, because the research says advisors trust curated software lists and Jump used that path.
Court outside compliance reviewers such as Synergy Compliance and XYPN compliance support, asking what they need to approve advisor software.
Use consumer provider labels in marketing and onboarding: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, with company names in parentheses.
insights: The research says herd safety matters: visible adopting-firm logos will eventually carry more weight than abstract security claims.
Microsoft adjacency matters because advisors already trust Microsoft 365 and OneDrive as accepted firm infrastructure.
The Compliance & Security pack is marketing, sales, and enablement at once: it gives an interested advisor something concrete to hand to the person who can block adoption.
Traffic tactics stay secondary until the demo and compliance story are ready; the current problem is not ad copy, it is trust and proof.

sections.title: Sales
sections.now: Sales is founder-led and proof-led. Start with the design partner, turn that into a live firm conversation, then use peer referrals and XYPN-style trust paths. The first sale is not a checkout-page problem; it is a permission, compliance, and live-demo problem.
decisions: Sell the compliance answer before the feature list: can the firm use it with client data, and can the CCO understand why?
Use the clean-slate Legion demo and the compliance-led onboarding as the primary sales conversation, not a static page.
Make the CCO pack the standard follow-up after an advisor shows interest.
Ask for design-partner proof first, then firm-level approval, then named references and peer introductions.
Treat booking-page deployment as a commercial launch action that needs explicit go-ahead before it is live.
insights: The design partner did not reject the product value; she hit the compliance gate first. That changes the order of the sale.
Support and onboarding matter: advisors expect a human setup path, not only self-serve software.
A firm CCO is a risk-minimizer and may not be deeply technical, so the sales material must explain data flow in plain English.
The product should sound serious enough for advisor software budgets, not like a cheap hobby tool.

sections.title: Growth & Traction
sections.now: Growth remains pre-revenue and near-zero traction, but the wedge is sharper: advisors want AI they are allowed to use with client data. The current growth plan is not a funnel. It is design-partner learning, compliance approval, firm proof, peer references, and XYPN-style distribution.
decisions: North Star: weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow.
First growth loop: design partner → firm approval → peer referrals → advisor group and XYPN trust paths.
Build a logo/reference wall only after real firms adopt; do not fake herd safety.
Validate demand through real advisor workflows and compliance conversations before widening traffic.
insights: The research confirms the old weak point and the new opening: advisors are already trying to use AI, but client-data rules block them from using generic ChatGPT plans.
XYPN and compliance consultants are leverage points because they reduce perceived risk for many small RIAs at once.
Pricing is still open; advisor software budgets support serious annual prices, but the first cohort should test willingness honestly.
Retention will come from repeated real workflows, not curiosity: meeting prep, cited answers, client-map updates, and approved AI use.

sections.title: Testing
sections.now: Current evidence: 7,108 tests plus guards green on the UI preview, real-Windows bench QA on the Legion, and the signed-installer pipeline validated. The R17 deep test covered onboarding, all three cloud AI providers, local AI, connectors, real file search, and real cited answers; four bugs were found and fixed. The final signed installer still waits on the pending Tauri version-align fix.

platforms.detail: The build machine runs the large automated suite. The latest UI preview passed 7,108 tests plus the guard checks, which means the codebase is broadly healthy before it goes to the real Windows bench.

Mac remains a secondary release confidence check. Keep Windows first because the advisor demo and most advisor environments run there; use the M1 bench before any broad Mac claim.

sections.title: Demo
sections.now: The current demo is the clean-slate Legion walkthrough for the design partner. The 2026-07-08 live walkthrough happened and drove the compliance reframe. The aha path is now: connect AI, import/connect practice data, watch progress, search, get a cited answer, and start a meeting with “⏺ Recording · Advisor Prep Hero” visible in the Notice Card.

steps.title: Start with the compliance promise
steps.do: Open the clean-slate demo. Show the restored intro and the new compliance-led story: the AI you are actually allowed to use with client data.
steps.say: Before we talk features, this answers the first question: can your firm use it? Your client files stay on your machine, and we give your compliance officer the data-flow pack.
steps.proves: The product understands the real buying gate before it asks for setup time.

steps.title: Connect AI without making it scary
steps.do: Show ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), and local AI as choices. Point out that the firm controls the account and key.
steps.say: Cloud AI means your own approved AI account; local AI means even the question stays on this computer. Either way, Lantern does not store your client files.
steps.proves: The privacy story is clear without accidentally making BYOK cloud mode feel unsafe.

steps.title: Connect practice data and build the map
steps.do: Use the clean connect step with M365, Gmail, OneDrive, and Wealthbox logos. Import files and let the progress screen run into a populated client view.
steps.say: This meets your data where it already lives: email, files, CRM notes, and client documents. It builds the Client Map from your own records.
steps.proves: The app is not asking the advisor to migrate their practice before seeing value.

steps.title: Ask, cite, and enter the meeting
steps.do: Ask a real pre-meeting question, open the cited source, then show the meeting surface with “⏺ Recording · Advisor Prep Hero” in the Notice Card.
steps.say: This is the core loop: ask the client file a question, verify the source, and walk into the meeting already oriented.
steps.proves: The product delivers the simple AI-first value: cited answers from client records, in the advisor workflow.

tips: Use the clean Legion state for the design-partner demo; old tokens and localStorage were cleared so the first-run path is real.
Lead with the compliance pack before the advisor gets nervous about AI keys.
Use consumer names for AI providers: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
End on a cited answer and the meeting Notice Card. That is the strongest “this is useful and allowed” moment.

sections.title: Finance & Metrics
sections.now: Keep the numbers honest: Lantern is still pre-revenue with near-zero traction. The current strategy exists because that was true. Pricing remains an open advisor-market question, and the first cohort should test a serious annual tier rather than inherit old pricing by default. The North Star is weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow.
decisions: Do not invent traction. Treat the business as pre-revenue until real advisors pay or sign.
Test higher advisor pricing; the source docs note advisors commonly spend thousands per year on software, so too-low pricing can signal “not serious.”
Keep the data guarantee: customers keep access to their files; paid features and updates can be gated, but their data is not hostage.
Defer SOC 2 spend until a real deal says it is the condition for signing.
insights: North Star metric: weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow.
Useful early funnel: design-partner walkthroughs, compliance-pack handoffs, firm approval conversations, demos, activated real-data workflows, weekly use, paid pilots, referrals.
Bring-your-own-key keeps AI costs low, but margin is not the hard part. Trust, approval, and repeated use are the hard parts.
Do not steer from made-up models. Re-run the financial model only after the first real cohort gives actual conversion, price, and retention data.

sections.now: These are the decisions actually waiting on Jameson now. They are about what goes live, what gets merged, and which go-to-market path to open next; routine build details stay with the AI team.

questions.answer: Recommendation: use the privacy-preserving Option A architecture, but get explicit go-ahead before live deploy because this is commercial-facing.

questions.q: Do our target users use Mac or Windows more?
questions.answer: Windows remains the priority for the advisor demo and real bench testing. Mac still matters, but Windows polish comes first.

questions.q: What else could I be doing with AI to push this project forward?
questions.answer: The still-valid answer: use AI to drive and test the real app, build a realistic advisor sample path, and support customer discovery and sales follow-up. Do not use it as an excuse to avoid talking to advisors.
